items.followUp: Define a strong electrolyte and give one example.

rubric.why: A weak electrolyte produces ions only partially in aqueous solution.
rubric.description: Defines a weak electrolyte as one that ionizes or dissociates only partially in solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating partial ionization or dissociation in solution.

rubric.why: Acetic acid and carbonic acid are weak electrolytes.
rubric.description: Gives a valid example of a weak electrolyte.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one correct example.

modelAnswer: A weak electrolyte is a substance that ionizes only partially in aqueous solution.

items.followUp: Write down two chemical properties of non-metals.

rubric.why: Metals react with oxygen to form metal oxides, which are generally basic.
rubric.description: States that metals react with oxygen to form metal oxides.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the reaction and product.

rubric.why: Many metals react with dilute acids to produce a salt and hydrogen gas.
rubric.description: States that many metals react with dilute acids to form a salt and hydrogen.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the reaction and products.

modelAnswer: Metals react with oxygen to form metal oxides, which are generally basic.
Many metals react with dilute acids to form a salt and hydrogen gas.

items.followUp: Write the chemical equations for magnesium reacting with oxygen and name the product.

rubric.why: Magnesium reacts with hot water to form magnesium hydroxide and hydrogen.
rubric.description: Writes the balanced equation for magnesium reacting with hot water.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct balanced equation.

rubric.why: Magnesium reacts with steam to form magnesium oxide and hydrogen.
rubric.description: Writes the balanced equation for magnesium reacting with steam.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct balanced equation.

modelAnswer: With hot water: Mg(s) + 2H₂O(l) → Mg(OH)₂(s) + H₂(g).
With steam: Mg(s) + H₂O(g) → MgO(s) + H₂(g).

items.followUp: Give four differences between an atom and a molecule.

rubric.why: A molecule has no net charge, whereas a molecular ion carries a net charge.
rubric.description: Contrasts the electrical charge of a molecule and a molecular ion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly stating both sides of the charge difference.

accept: formed by gaining or losing electrons
rubric.why: A molecular ion results when a bonded group of atoms gains or loses electrons; a molecule is neutral.
rubric.description: Distinguishes a neutral molecule from a molecular ion formed by electron gain or loss.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a molecular ion forms through electron gain or loss.

rubric.why: Molecular-ion formulas show their ionic charge, unlike neutral molecule formulas.
rubric.description: Contrasts how the formulas of molecules and molecular ions are written.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly describing charge notation for both.

rubric.why: H₂O is a molecule and NH₄⁺, SO₄²⁻, NO₃⁻, and OH⁻ are molecular ions.
rubric.description: Gives a correct molecule and a correct molecular-ion example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one correct example of each.

modelAnswer: A molecule is electrically neutral, whereas a molecular ion carries a net positive or negative charge.
A molecular ion is formed when a bonded group of atoms gains or loses electrons; a molecule is a neutral particle.
A molecule’s formula is written without an ionic charge, while a molecular ion’s formula shows its charge.
Examples: H₂O is a molecule; NH₄⁺ is a molecular ion.
